history: Established by the African Union through a statute adopted in 2018 to coordinate Africa's space activities and policies. Its headquarters in Cairo, Egypt, were inaugurated on 20 April 2025. It works alongside national agencies to implement the African Space Policy and Strategy.
key_people: Tidiane Ouattara, President of the African Space Council (appointed 2024); Director General position not yet filled as of September 2026
specialties: Regional coordination; African Space Policy and Strategy
notable_missions: African Space Policy and Strategy coordination; regional data programmes
launch_capability: No indigenous orbital launcher; coordination body, not a launching entity
notes: Multinational agency of the African Union. AU procurement documents list AU tender contacts, not an AfSA general office phone/email, so those fields are left blank.

agency_name: Agencia Espacial Costarricense (Costa Rican Space Agency, AEC)
history: Created by Law 9960, passed by the Legislative Assembly on February 8, 2021 and signed March 27, 2021, as a non-state public entity with technical, administrative and management autonomy, subject to the guidelines of the Ministry of Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications (MICITT). Governed by a five-member Board of Directors chaired ex officio by the MICITT minister, it is the first space agency created and operated by a Central American nation.
key_people: Five-member Board of Directors chaired ex officio by the Minister of MICITT (Paula Bogantes Zamora, Minister of MICITT, as of September 2026); no named Executive Director verified
specialties: space policy and regulation (authorization and supervision of national space activities); space research and innovation; aerospace ecosystem development
notable_missions: None flown yet; mandate includes the Guanacaste Space Center project (Liberia) and a national registry of space objects
notes: First Central American national space agency. Law 9960 funded the agency for five years via contributions from non-financial public-sector institutions (est. ₡2-3B total over 2021-2025 per legislative debate); no published annual budget found. MICITT advertised an Executive Director competition in 2023; no named executive director could be verified on official pages as of September 2026. No standalone official website, published phone, or general email verified - communications run through MICITT (micitt.go.cr).

history: The Agencia Espacial Espanola was created by Law 17/2022 and held its constitutive board session in Seville on 20 April 2023. It is Spain's national body for space security, scientific research, industry promotion and coordination of national institutions in space matters. It designs and coordinates the Spanish Space Strategy and represents Spain at ESA and EUSPA.
key_people: Juan Carlos Cortes Pulido, Director (per ESA, May 2026)
specialties: Space strategy, space security, Earth observation, space surveillance (S3TOC), industry coordination
notable_missions: Paz (Earth observation), Spainsat NG programme, national SST operations (S3TOC)
notes: Spain's space coordination was previously led by INTA/CDTI; AEE is the current national coordinating agency. HQ: C/ Jose Galan Merino 6, 41015 Seville (from official state procurement notices). No general public email published (only a procurement mailbox). 2026 budget not published.

history: Created by the Law creating the Mexican Space Agency, published by President Felipe Calderón on July 30, 2010 (in force July 31, 2010); its first Governing Board was formed on September 7, 2010, and its first Director General, Francisco Javier Mendieta Jiménez, took office November 1, 2011. A successor to the 1962-1977 Comisión Nacional del Espacio Exterior (CONEE), AEM coordinates Mexico's space policy, research and education activities; in 2025 its attributions began being integrated into the Agencia de Transformación Digital y Telecomunicaciones (ATDT).
key_people: Director General post vacant since February 2025: Salvador Landeros Ayala (confirmed for 2023-2027) resigned; no successor named
budget_usd: MXN 63.6M (~US$3.2M), 2021; no newer published budget found
specialties: space policy coordination; Earth observation; satellite communications policy; nanosatellites; STEM education
notable_missions: Nanoconect-1 stratospheric payload (2017); AztechSat-1 CubeSat (deployed from the ISS, Dec 2019); Mexican command-and-management payload for nanosatellites slated for Paraguay's GuaraniSat-2 (Oct 2025); Tulancingo I radiotelescope project
notes: Per a 2025 ATDT press release, after Director General Salvador Landeros Ayala's resignation, the ATDT's General Satellite Directorate assumed/integrated AEM's and MEXSAT's attributions; AEM's powers 'do not disappear' but are being exercised via the ATDT. Phone and general email not found on official pages as of September 2026.

history: Created by presidential decree on 16 January 2002 to develop Algeria's national space programme. It operates the Oran satellite development centre and the national Earth observation programme. It is the national authority for space activities.
key_people: Azzedine Oussedik, Director General
specialties: Earth observation; satellite development
notable_missions: Alsat-1 (2002); Alsat-2A/2B; Alsat-3B (2023)
launch_capability: No indigenous orbital launcher; missions use commercial and foreign launch providers
notes: No agency-specific annual budget is officially published; the field is left blank.

agency_name: Arthur C. Clarke Institute for Modern Technologies (ACCIMT)
founded: 1984 (as the Arthur C. Clarke Centre for Modern Technologies, Act No. 30 of 1984; reconstituted as the Institute under the Science and Technology Development Act No. 11 of 1994)
history: Established in 1984 by an Act of Parliament as the Arthur C. Clarke Centre for Modern Technologies, endowed with Sir Arthur C. Clarke's Marconi Prize award money; it was reconstituted as the Institute under the 1994 Science and Technology Development Act. It is Sri Lanka's statutory national institute for modern technologies including space applications, space science, and remote sensing, and is the national focal point for space technology applications (UNESCAP). It develops nanosatellites with Japan (Kyutech/JAXA), including Raavana-1 and DRAGON FLY.
key_people: Eng. (Dr.) Sanath Panawennage, Director General and CEO (per March 2024 official material)
specialties: space applications and remote sensing; electronics and communications; astronomy and space science
notable_missions: Raavana-1 (Sri Lanka's first nanosatellite, 2019); DRAGON FLY nanosatellite (2025); KITSUNE participation
notes: A statutory technology institute rather than a dedicated space agency; included as Sri Lanka's national space institution. The general line is from the institute's 2021 annual report; the email shown there (info@accmt.ac.lk) appears to be a misprint and is not used. Leader currency as of September 2026 not re-verified.

history: Established on 1 July 2018 as Australia's national civil space agency, headquartered in Adelaide within the Department of Industry, Science and Resources. It coordinates national space policy, regulates commercial launch and re-entry activities, and grows the domestic space industry. It administers national space programs and industry-support measures.
key_people: Enrico Palermo, Head of the Agency (since 28 January 2021)
specialties: space regulation and licensing; industry development; international partnerships; Earth observation
notable_missions: No sovereign spacecraft; supports and regulates commercial missions, including Australia's first domestic orbital-launch attempts
launch_capability: None sovereign; licensed commercial launches from Australian soil
notes: The 2026–27 federal budget provides A$21.7M over two years for core agency functions — a two-year measure rather than a published annual agency budget — so budget_usd is left blank rather than annualized.

history: Austria's space activities are handled by the Aeronautics and Space Agency, part of the Austrian Research Promotion Agency (FFG). The agency implements Austria's aerospace strategy, manages ESA and EU programme participation, and funds national aerospace research. Austria has been an ESA member since 1987.
key_people: Andreas Geisler, Head of the Aerospace Agency (per official event materials; currency unconfirmed)
specialties: Aerospace research funding, ESA programme management, aeronautics, space applications
notable_missions: Austrian instruments on ESA missions (e.g. CHEOPS contribution), BRITE-Austria/TUGSAT-1 nanosatellite, national ASAP programme
notes: Founded 1972 as the Austrian Space Agency; integrated into FFG in 2005. FFG itself is jointly managed by Henrietta Egerth and Karin Tausz. Functional mailbox ALR@ffg.at per ESA national-agencies contact list; no published switchboard.

history: Established by Royal Decree No. 11 of 2014 as the National Space Science Agency (NSSA). It was renamed the Bahrain Space Agency by Royal Decree No. 14 of 2025. It works under the supervision of the Supreme Defence Council on space science, capacity building and Earth observation services.
key_people: Mohamed Ebrahim Al Aseeri, Chief Executive Officer
specialties: Space science; capacity building; Earth observation services
notable_missions: Light-1 cubesat (2021, with the UAE); multispectral camera aboard China's Chang'e-7 lunar mission (2026)
notes: No agency-specific annual budget is officially published; the field is left blank. The official website URL was not verified in the current research sweep and is left blank.

agency_name: Bangladesh Space Research and Remote Sensing Organization (SPARRSO)
founded: 1980 (created by merging the Satellite Research Centre (SARC) and the Bangladesh Landsat Program)
history: Created in 1980 by merging the Satellite Research Centre (SARC) and the Bangladesh Landsat Program (BLP). An autonomous organization under the Ministry of Defence, it is Bangladesh's national body for space research and remote-sensing applications. It supplies satellite-based data, information, and maps to ministries and agencies.
key_people: Md Rashedul Islam, Chairman
specialties: remote sensing; satellite applications; space and atmospheric science
notable_missions: No sovereign satellites; Bangladesh's first satellite, Bangabandhu-1 (2018), is operated by the telecom regulator (BTRC), not SPARRSO
notes: The annual report lists the chairman's office contact, which is excluded here (personal/direct contacts); no general public phone or email is published. In June 2026 the prime minister visited SPARRSO headquarters and directed its modernization.

agency_name: BELSPO - DG Space Research and Applications
history: Belgium's civil space activities are administered by the Belgian Federal Science Policy Office (BELSPO), whose Space Research and Applications directorate manages national space policy. BELSPO coordinates Belgium's participation in ESA programmes and funds national space research. Belgium has been an ESA member since its founding and hosts the B-USOC operations centre.
specialties: Space policy administration, ESA programme coordination, Earth observation applications, space law
notable_missions: PROBA series (Belgian-led ESA missions), Belgian ESA astronaut activities, B-USOC ISS operations support
notes: Belgium has no standalone space agency; BELSPO is the national civil-space authority. No published director of the space directorate found; ESA's Belgium page cites Jean-Francois Mayence (BELSPO Legal Unit - International Relations) for space-law matters. No general email published.

history: Created by law approved on 9 August 2007 and officially published on 25 October 2007; operations began on 1 January 2008 as the Bolivarian Agency for Space Activities. It develops national satellite programmes and applications. It is headquartered in Caracas.
specialties: Satellite programmes; space applications
notable_missions: Venesat-1 (2008); VRSS-1 (2012) and VRSS-2 (2017)
notes: Current 2026 leadership not verified in official sources; the field is left blank.

history: Created by Supreme Decree No. 0423 on 10 February 2010 as the Bolivian Space Agency. It operates Bolivia's national communications satellite. It manages the Amachuma ground station near La Paz.
specialties: Satellite communications operations
notable_missions: Tupac Katari (TKSAT-1, 2013)
launch_capability: No indigenous orbital launcher; satellite launched and operated via international partners
notes: Current 2026 leadership not verified in official sources; the field is left blank.

history: Created by law on 10 February 1994 as Brazil's national civil space agency, succeeding earlier space programmes under the National Commission for Space Activities. It implements the National Space Activities Programme (PNAE). It operates from Brasília with the Alcantara Launch Center.
key_people: Marco Antonio Chamon, President
specialties: Satellite development; launch infrastructure; international cooperation
notable_missions: CBERS programme (with China); Amazonia-1 (2021)
launch_capability: No operational indigenous orbital launcher; Alcantara Launch Center used for suborbital and foreign partner launches
notes: No agency-specific annual budget is officially published as a stand-alone figure; the field is left blank.

agency_name: BRIN – Research Organization for Aeronautics and Space (ORPA)
founded: 2021 (ORPA formed within BRIN; LAPAN space heritage dates to 1963)
history: Indonesia's space heritage dates to the National Institute of Aeronautics and Space (LAPAN), founded in 1963. In 2021 LAPAN was integrated into the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN), and its space research functions became the Research Organization for Aeronautics and Space (ORPA). A separate Indonesian Space Agency secretariat (INASA) within BRIN coordinates the national registry of space objects.
key_people: Robertus Heru Triharjanto, Head of ORPA
specialties: aeronautics and space research; satellite development; rocketry research
notable_missions: LAPAN-A1, LAPAN-A2, and LAPAN-A3 satellites; proposed Biak spaceport
notes: INASA's published contact (space@brin.go.id) belongs to the space-object registry coordination, not to ORPA's general public contact, so email is left blank. INASA was designated registry coordinator under a BRIN decree.

agency_name: Canadian Space Agency / Agence spatiale canadienne (CSA)
history: Established by the Canadian Space Agency Act (royal assent 1990), formally created in March 1989; its headquarters, the John H. Chapman Space Centre in Longueuil, Quebec, opened in 1992. Canada's earlier space heritage includes the Alouette-1 satellite (1962) and the Canadarm on the Space Shuttle; milestones since include Marc Garneau's flight (1984), RADARSAT-1 (1995), Chris Hadfield commanding the ISS (2013), and Canadian participation in the Artemis program, including Jeremy Hansen on Artemis II (April 2026).
key_people: Jean-Claude Piedboeuf, Acting President (since July 2026; previously Senior Vice-President, Space Programs). Lisa Campbell's term (2020-2025, extended to September 2026) ended early; Piedboeuf became the agency's eighth acting president.
budget_usd: ≈US$660M (CA$913.9M planned spending, FY2026–27 Departmental Plan — $857.1M core responsibilities + $56.9M internal services)
specialties: human spaceflight participation; space robotics; Earth observation; space science and technology; satellite communications and applications
notable_missions: RADARSAT Constellation Mission; Canadarm2 (ISS); Canadarm3 (Lunar Gateway); Artemis II (Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen, first Canadian on a crewed lunar mission, April 2026); WildFireSat
launch_capability: None (relies on international partners and commercial launch providers)
notes: Reports to the Minister of Industry (Hon. Mélanie Joly per the 2025-26 Departmental Plan). Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen announced in July 2026 that he would step back from a full-time astronaut role in September 2026. No permanent CSA president had been announced as of the 13 Oct 2026 check; the search opened in April 2026
column15: and Minister Melanie Joly said (early Oct 2026) a new president would be announced in the coming weeks - Piedboeuf remains acting.

history: Founded on 19 December 1961 by General de Gaulle, CNES is the French government agency that proposes France's space policy and implements it in Europe. It designs and orbits satellites, invents the space systems of the future and nurtures new space-based services. CNES operates four centres of excellence, including the Guiana Space Centre in Kourou.
key_people: Francois Jacq, Chairman and CEO (appointed 15 April 2026 for five years; had led CNES since 23 May 2025)
budget_usd: approx $2.7-2.8B (France civil space spend approx EUR 2.3-2.4B/yr per 2025 government figures; converted at EUR1=$1.17; CNES's own 2026 budget not separately published)
specialties: Launch systems, Earth observation, space science, telecommunications, defence space, space applications
notable_missions: Ariane programme, SPOT, Pleiades Neo, Jason series, SuperCam (Mars 2020 contribution), Euclid contribution
launch_capability: None (indigenous orbital launcher); operates the Guiana Space Centre; orbital access via ESA's Ariane 6 and Vega C
notes: HQ: 2, place Maurice Quentin, Paris (switchboard from official CNES brochure). General enquiries via website forms; no general email published.

history: Established on 22 April 1993 as China's national civilian space authority, succeeding the space functions of the former Ministry of Aerospace Industry. It sets national space policy and runs the lunar, planetary, and Earth-observation programs, while crewed spaceflight is managed separately by the China Manned Space Engineering Office. Landmark programs include the Chang'e lunar missions, the Tianwen-1 Mars mission, and the Tiangong space station.
key_people: Shan Zhongde, Administrator (confirmed in an official Chinese government release, April 2026)
specialties: lunar and planetary exploration; launch vehicles; Earth observation; satellite navigation
notable_missions: Chang'e 4 (first lunar far-side landing); Chang'e 5 and 6 (lunar sample return); Tianwen-1 and the Zhurong Mars rover; Tiangong space station; BeiDou navigation system
launch_capability: Long March rocket family, launched from Jiuquan, Taiyuan, Xichang, and Wenchang
notes: China publishes no clean CNSA-only annual budget; figures in secondary sources (e.g., a frequently cited 2023 figure near US$18B, Wikipedia, not an official CNSA figure) refer to overall government space spending and are not used here. No general public HQ phone or general email is published; only mission-specific contacts appear on the official site.

history: Created by Presidential Decree 2442 in July 2006 as Colombia's official intersectoral body for consultation, coordination and planning of the national space policy. It brings together government entities involved in space activities. It is the national focal point for Colombia's space policy.
specialties: Space policy coordination
notable_missions: National space policy coordination; Libertad-1 (2007) and Libertad-2 university cubesats
notes: Colombia's official national space body is the intersectoral commission; a private non-profit calling itself the Agencia Espacial de Colombia is excluded. Current secretariat leadership not verified.

history: Created in June 2025 as Côte d'Ivoire's national space agency. Its inaugural Director General, Dr Tidiane Ouattara, was appointed in August 2026. The agency is beginning the country's institutional space programme, including capacity building and international cooperation.
key_people: Tidiane Ouattara, Director General (appointed August 2026)
specialties: Capacity building; international cooperation
notable_missions: Côte d'Ivoire signed the Artemis Accords (September 2026)
notes: Newly established agency (2025); no budget or contact details officially published yet.

agency_name: Czech Space Office / Ministry of Transport - Department of Space Activities
history: The Czech Space Office was founded in 2003 as a non-profit association supporting Czech space activities. Since 2011 national space authority rests with the Ministry of Transport's Department of Space Activities, which coordinates Czech space policy and ESA participation. Czechia joined ESA in 2008.
key_people: Vaclav Kobera, Director of the Department of Space Activities, Ministry of Transport (per Czech Space Portal, January 2026)
specialties: Space policy coordination, ESA/EU programme management, national space portal
notable_missions: Czech ESA contributions, VZLUSAT series, national small-satellite projects
notes: The Czech Space Office is an association, not a state agency; state authority sits with the Ministry of Transport since 2011. Phone and email are the ministry's published general contacts.

agency_name: Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science - Space Division
history: Denmark has no standalone space agency; space policy is coordinated by the Ministry of Higher Education and Science through the Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science, which has housed a space division since 2016. A royal decree of 8 May 2015 placed coordination of space activities under the ministry. In November 2024 Denmark adopted a national strategy for space research and innovation towards 2035.
key_people: Christina Egelund, Minister of Higher Education and Science (space portfolio; 2024 strategy)
specialties: Space research funding, ESA coordination, national space programme, DTU Space national institute
notable_missions: Danish ESA contributions, DTU Space instruments (e.g. ASIM on ISS, Swarm contribution), proposed Mani ESA mission lead
notes: ESA membership handled by the ministry; DTU Space is Denmark's national space institute. Phone and email are the ministry's published general contacts. No standalone agency budget.

history: Established by law in January 2018 as Egypt's national space agency. It succeeded earlier national space programmes with a mandate to create, transfer and localize space technology. Its headquarters in Cairo's 5th Settlement also hosts the African Space Agency.
key_people: Maged Ismail, Chief Executive Officer (appointed August 2025; active September 2026)
specialties: Satellite development; technology localization; Earth observation
notable_missions: Horus-1 and Horus-2; MisrSat-2; NExSat-1
launch_capability: No indigenous orbital launcher; missions use commercial and foreign launch providers
notes: No agency-specific annual budget is officially published; the field is left blank. Website, switchboard and general email as published in the agency's International Astronautical Federation member listing (verified 2026-09-26).

agency_name: El Salvador Aerospace Institute (Instituto Aerospacial de El Salvador, ESAI)
history: Founded in 2012 by Dr. Luis Alfaro as a Salvadoran aerospace think tank; launched a Global Aerospace program in 2016 and participates in international aerospace cooperation (UNOOSA, UNISEC-Global). It claims authorization by national decree to lead the country's National Aerospace Plan and describes itself as El Salvador's national space agency (designation claimed September 7, 2021); it was not created by statute and the claimed government decree could not be independently verified.
key_people: Dr. Luis Alfaro, President and Founder
specialties: aerospace R&D and innovation; STEM education programs; national aerospace program planning; international cooperation
notable_missions: Global Aerospace Program (first launch activity, 2016); National Aerospace Plan; South Korean space-program training participation
notes: Private, non-governmental institute rather than a statutory agency; its claimed national-agency status by government decree is self-asserted on its own site and was not independently verified against an official government act. No published budget, phone, or general email found on its official site as of September 2026.

history: Ireland has no standalone space agency; national space activities and ESA participation are administered by Enterprise Ireland, the state enterprise agency. It manages Ireland's ESA programme engagement and supports Irish space-industry development. Ireland has been an ESA member since 1980.
key_people: Conor Sheehan, Irish Delegation to ESA (per ESA, 2026)
specialties: ESA programme management, space-industry development, technology transfer
notable_missions: Irish ESA contributions, EIRSAT-1 (Ireland's first satellite, 2023), national ESA BIC activities
notes: 2026 reporting cites a EUR 170M five-year ESA commitment; official budget basis not confirmed. Functional mailbox SciSpacE@enterpriseireland.com per ESA national-agencies list; no published switchboard.

agency_name: Ethiopian Space Science and Geospatial Institute (SSGI)
history: Successor to the Ethiopian Space Science and Technology Institute (founded 2016), reorganized as the Space Science and Geospatial Institute. It develops national space and geospatial capabilities. It operated Ethiopia's first satellite programmes.
key_people: Abdisa Yilma, Director General
specialties: Space science; geospatial applications; satellite programmes
notable_missions: ETRSS-1 (2019); ESSTI-II (2020)
notes: No agency-specific annual budget is officially published; the field is left blank.

history: ESA was formed in 1975 through the merger of the European Space Research Organisation (ESRO) and the European Launcher Development Organisation (ELDO). It is an intergovernmental organisation dedicated to the exploration of space, with a mandate to shape the development of Europe's space capability. ESA's programmes cover human and robotic exploration, Earth observation, navigation, telecommunications, technology and space science.
key_people: Josef Aschbacher, Director General (mandate renewed for four years from 1 March 2025)
specialties: Space science, human and robotic exploration, Earth observation, navigation, telecommunications, launchers, technology development
notable_missions: Ariane 6, Vega C, Galileo, Copernicus/Sentinels, Rosetta, BepiColombo, Euclid, JUICE, Gaia
notes: Country field follows the assigned convention. Note: ESA itself reported Slovenia as its 23rd Member State from 1 January 2025. No published HQ switchboard or general email found; contact via online forms.

agency_name: Finnish Space Office (Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment)
history: Finland's space administration is coordinated by the Finnish Space Office, hosted by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment. The office heads the secretariat of the national Space Committee, coordinates delegations to ESA and the EU, and maintains national space legislation and the space-object register. Finland joined ESA in 1995.
key_people: Tero Vihavainen, Secretary General of the Finnish Space Committee (Chief Specialist, Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment; per ministry page)
specialties: Space policy coordination, ESA/EU representation, space legislation and authorisation, industry communications
notable_missions: Finnish ESA contributions, Aalto-1/Aalto-2 and Suomi 100 national satellites, ICEYE commercial constellation
notes: No standalone agency; business-support functions sit with Business Finland. 2026 budget not published. No published space-office switchboard or general email located.

agency_name: Gabonese Agency for Space Studies and Observations (AGEOS)
history: Gabon's Agency for Space Studies and Observations, the national Earth-observation agency. It develops satellite imagery applications for forestry, environment and land management. It hosted the NewSpace Africa Conference 2026 in Gabon.
key_people: Aboubakar Mambimba Ndjoungui, Director General
specialties: Earth observation; environmental monitoring
notable_missions: National Earth observation programme; NewSpace Africa Conference 2026 host
notes: No agency-specific annual budget is officially published; the field is left blank.

agency_name: General Satellite Directorate, Agency for Digital Transformation and Telecommunications (ATDT)
history: The Mexican Space Agency (AEM) was created in 2010 as a decentralized federal entity. After the resignation of its Director General Salvador Landeros in January 2025, the Agency for Digital Transformation and Telecommunications (ATDT) created a General Satellite Directorate integrating the attributions of the AEM and the Mexican Satellite System (MEXSAT). The powers of the AEM were retained within this new structure.
key_people: Jose Antonio Pena Merino, head of the ATDT
specialties: Satellite communications; digital inclusion; space talent
notable_missions: AztechSat-1 (2019); MEXSAT satellites; planned geostationary telecommunications satellite
notes: The AEM was dissolved as an independent agency in 2025; its functions were absorbed by the ATDT's General Satellite Directorate. No agency-specific annual budget is officially published.

agency_name: Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA)
history: Founded on 3 November 2000 as Thailand's national space and geoinformatics agency, building on Thai remote-sensing activity that began with participation in NASA's ERTS program in 1971. It operates the THEOS Earth-observation satellites and provides satellite data and geospatial services for disaster monitoring, agriculture, and resource management. It is headquartered in Bangkok.
key_people: Dr. Pakorn Apaphant, Executive Director
specialties: Earth observation; geoinformatics; disaster and resource monitoring
notable_missions: THEOS-1 (Thaichote); THEOS-2 and THEOS-2A (launched 2023)
notes: info@gistda.or.th is widely corroborated (USGS, IAF) but was not captured directly from GISTDA's current contact page; no official HQ switchboard found.

history: DLR is Germany's national research centre for aeronautics and space and the country's space agency. Its roots go back to 1969 with the founding of the DFVLR; today's DLR was formed in 1997 from the merger of Germany's space organisations. On behalf of the German government, DLR plans and implements the national space programme and represents Germany at ESA.
key_people: Anke Kaysser-Pyzalla, Chair of the Executive Board (reappointed December 2024 for 2025-2030)
budget_usd: approx $0.64B (2026 federal institutional grant of EUR 550M in draft budget, reported 2026; full 2026 agency budget not published; converted at EUR1=$1.17)
specialties: Aeronautics, space research, energy, transport, security; manages German ESA contributions
notable_missions: TerraSAR-X/TanDEM-X, EnMAP, Columbus module (ISS), Philae lander contribution, GRACE-FO
launch_capability: None (indigenous orbital launcher); sounding rockets via MORABA; supports German commercial microlauncher initiatives
notes: Founded 1969 as DFVLR; current DLR structure dates to 1997. 2026 federal core funding faced a reported EUR 21M shortfall in draft budget negotiations. No published HQ switchboard or general email found.

agency_name: Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI)
history: Established in 2012 under the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission as the national institution for space science and technology. It leads Ghana's satellite and radio astronomy programmes. A proposed Ghana Space Agency had not been legally established as of September 2026, so this official institute is listed.
key_people: Joseph Bremang Tandoh, Director
specialties: Space science; satellite development; radio astronomy
notable_missions: GhanaSat-1 (2017, with Japan)
notes: This is an official institute, not a full national space agency; no stand-alone budget is officially published. Cabinet approved (2 Oct 2026) converting GSSTI into a Ghana Space Agency with the enabling legislation being drafted per the Environment, Science and Technology minister's 2 Oct 2026 announcement - not yet legally established as of the 13 Oct 2026 check.

history: The Hellenic Space Center was established in 2018 as Greece's national space body under the Ministry of Digital Governance. It coordinates national space policy, manages the HELLAS-SPACE national programme, and represents Greece at ESA. Greece has been an ESA member since 2005.
key_people: Dr Emmanuel Rammos, President (per official HSC page, 2026)
specialties: National space programme management, Earth observation, satellite communications, space applications
notable_missions: HELLAS-SPACE programme, Greek ESA contributions, national small-satellite initiatives
notes: In 2026 Greece announced the approx EUR 350M four-year HELLAS-SPACE 2.0 programme (not an annual agency budget). Annual budget not published.

history: Hungary's space activities are coordinated through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, which hosts the national space office function. Hungary participates in ESA as a full member since 2015 and pursues a national space strategy focused on industry and research. Space affairs are led by a ministerial commissioner for space research.
key_people: Orsolya Ferencz, Ministerial Commissioner for Space Research (per 2025-2026 materials)
specialties: Space policy, ESA coordination, national space strategy, Hunor astronaut programme
notable_missions: Hungarian ESA contributions, Hunor programme (Hungarian astronaut to ISS, 2025), Masat-1 (first Hungarian satellite, 2012)
notes: No standalone agency identified; functions sit within the ministry. 2026 budget and leadership currency not confirmed. No published switchboard or general email located.

history: Founded on 15 August 1969 as the successor to the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR, 1962). It runs India's satellite, launch-vehicle, and planetary programs and is one of the few agencies worldwide with full end-to-end launch capability. IN-SPACe, a separate body under the Department of Space, authorizes and promotes private-sector space activity.
key_people: V. Narayanan, Chairman (in office since 14 January 2025)
budget_usd: ≈US$1.46B (₹13,705.60 crore, FY2026–27 Department of Space allocation)
specialties: launch vehicles; Earth observation; satellite navigation (NavIC); planetary science; human spaceflight (Gaganyaan)
notable_missions: Chandrayaan-3 (lunar south-pole landing, 2023); Aditya-L1 (solar observatory); Gaganyaan crew program; SpaDeX (orbital docking demonstration)
launch_capability: PSLV, GSLV, and LVM3 in operational service; SSLV; crewed Gaganyaan launches planned
notes: The budget figure is the Department of Space's full allocation, not an ISRO-only operating budget; the USD equivalent follows 2026 reporting.

agency_name: Interministerial Board for Space Policy (Junta Interministerial de Politica Espacial)
history: Created by Decree 71/2022 as Uruguay's interministerial board for national space policy. It coordinates the ministries involved in space activities. In 2026 Uruguay reported to the UN that institutional changes were expected during the year; a proposed Uruguayan Space Agency had not been enacted.
specialties: National space policy coordination
notable_missions: National space policy coordination; UNOOSA 2026 statement on institutional reform
notes: Uruguay's official national space body is the interministerial board; no current chair verified in official sources.

history: Established under legislation passed in 2003 and operating from 2004 as Iran's civil space agency under the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology. It develops national satellites, ground infrastructure and space applications. Orbital launch operations are conducted by separate defence-sector organisations.

specialties: Satellite development; ground systems; space applications
notable_missions: Omid (2009); Nahid series; Khayyam (2022, launched by Russia)
launch_capability: Limited: the agency develops satellites and ground systems; orbital launches are carried out by separate defence-sector organisations, not the civil agency
notes: No agency-specific annual budget is officially published; the field is left blank.

history: Founded in 1983 under the Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology to initiate and coordinate Israel's civil space programme. It supports the development of satellite and launcher technologies and international cooperation. Ran Livne was appointed director for a four-year term in April 2026.
key_people: Ran Livne, Director (appointed April 2026 for a four-year term)
specialties: Satellite and launcher technology; international cooperation

notes: No agency-specific annual budget is officially published; the field is left blank.

history: ASI was established in 1988 as a government agency to unify Italy's space efforts and coordinate national space policy. It defines and implements Italy's civil space programme and represents Italy within ESA, where Italy is the third-largest contributor. ASI oversees the Centre for Space Geodesy in Matera and the Broglio Space Centre in Malindi, Kenya.
key_people: Amb. Mario Cospito, Extraordinary Commissioner (appointed 8 August 2026, per ASI's official announcement; in office until the new president and board take office, max 12 months). Luca Vincenzo Maria Salamone, Director General (appointed 14 November 2023)
budget_usd: approx $0.53B (2026 ASI financing fund of EUR 450.35M per Italy's 2026 Budget Law via presidenza.governo.it; Italy's total civil space spend approx EUR 2.3-2.4B/yr; converted at EUR1=$1.17)

Mario Cospito was appointed extraordinary commissioner on 8 August 2026 (announced by ASI and the Minister for Enterprises and Made in Italy), exercising ordinary and extraordinary administration until the new president and board are seated. No published HQ switchboard or general email found.

founded: 2003 (1 October 2003; merger of NASDA, ISAS, and NAL)
history: Formed on 1 October 2003 by merging the National Space Development Agency (NASDA), the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS), and the National Aerospace Laboratory (NAL). It covers Japan's full space program — launch vehicles, space science, human spaceflight, and Earth observation — centered on the Tsukuba Space Center. Its H3 heavy-lift rocket entered operational service in 2024.
key_people: Hiroshi Yamakawa, President (in office through at least July 2026)

notes: No official standalone annual agency budget found in English sources; a FY2025 figure of ¥154.5 billion appeared only in a nonofficial source and is not used. No published general HQ switchboard or general public email could be verified.

agency_name: JSC National Company Kazakhstan Gharysh Sapary
history: Established by government decree on 17 March 2005 as Kazakhstan's national space company. It operates the KazEOSat Earth-observation satellites and provides geospatial and remote-sensing services, reporting through the government's aerospace governance structure. It is headquartered in Astana.

history: Established in 2017 as the national space agency under the Ministry of Defence. It implements Kenya's national space programme and regulates space activities. It operates the Malindi ground station in partnership with international agencies.
key_people: Hillary Kipkosgey, Director General (Brigadier)
specialties: Earth observation; satellite regulation; space applications
launch_capability: No indigenous orbital launcher; missions use commercial and foreign launch providers

history: Established on 27 May 2024 as South Korea's first dedicated national space agency, headquartered in Sacheon. It consolidated space-policy, program, and R&D functions previously spread across ministries and oversees the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) and the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute (KASI), which continue as affiliated institutes. Founding Administrator Yoon Young-bin was succeeded by Oh Tae-seok (Oh Taeseog) during 2026.

specialties: national space policy; launch-vehicle development; satellite programs; lunar exploration; international cooperation

notes: The USD figure follows 2026 Korean reporting; KRW–USD equivalents vary with the conversion rate used. No general public email found on the official site.

agency_name: Latin American and Caribbean Space Agency (ALCE)
history: Created at the CELAC summit in Mexico City in September 2021; its constitutive convention was published in Mexico's Official Gazette in April 2022. It is the intergovernmental regional space organization for Latin America and the Caribbean, headquartered in Queretaro, Mexico. ESA hosted ALCE alongside AfSA and APSCO for the first joint regional space agencies meeting in May 2026.
key_people: Oscar Freddy Gonzalez Rivera, Secretary General
specialties: Regional cooperation; satellite communications; disaster management
notable_missions: MoU with the International Deep Space Exploration Association on deep-space cooperation (2026); 21+ member states
launch_capability: No indigenous orbital launcher; coordination body, not a launching entity
notes: Multinational agency. No budget, phone or general email officially published; the fields are left blank.

history: The Latvian Space Office operates under Latvia's Ministry of Economics as the national contact for space matters. It coordinates Latvia's engagement with ESA, with which Latvia holds associate cooperation status progressing toward fuller membership. The office promotes Latvian space industry and research participation in European programmes.
specialties: ESA cooperation coordination, industry liaison
notable_missions: Latvian ESA cooperation activities, Venta-1 satellite (2017, with industry)
notes: Details limited in located materials; listed by ESA among national space offices. No leadership, budget, or contacts published in located sources.

history: The Lithuanian Space Office operates within the Agency for Science, Innovation and Technology (MITA) as the national space contact. It coordinates Lithuania's cooperation with ESA under associate status and supports Lithuanian participation in European space programmes. Lithuania signed an Association Agreement with ESA in 2021.
specialties: ESA cooperation coordination, innovation support
notable_missions: Lithuanian ESA cooperation activities, LituanicaSAT and LitSat student satellites (2014)
notes: Details limited in located materials; listed by ESA among national space offices. No leadership, budget, or contacts published in located sources.

history: The Luxembourg Space Agency was established in 2018 by the Ministry of the Economy to develop the national space sector. It fosters new and existing companies, develops human resources, facilitates access to funding and supports academic research. It implements the national space economic development strategy and leads the SpaceResources.lu initiative.
key_people: Ruy Pinto, Interim CEO (appointed 14 September 2026 for an initial six months, succeeding Marc Serres; per Luxembourg government release)
specialties: Space economic development, space resources, commercial space, skills and research funding
notable_missions: National LuxIMPULSE and R&D programmes, SpaceResources.lu initiative, ESA/EU programme participation
notes: Placed under the authority of the Ministry of the Economy. 2026 budget not published. No published HQ switchboard or general email located.

founded: 2019 (approved by cabinet 20 February 2019; merger of ANGKASA and the Malaysian Remote Sensing Agency)
history: Created on 20 February 2019 by merging the Malaysian National Space Agency (ANGKASA) and the Malaysian Remote Sensing Agency (MRSA). It implements the National Space Policy 2030, operates satellite-data services, and develops the domestic space industry. It is headquartered in Kuala Lumpur.
key_people: Azlikamil Napiah, Director General (current through at least August 2026)

notable_missions: RazakSAT (2009); TiungSAT-1 (2000, predecessor ANGKASA era); ongoing Earth-observation satellite program

history: The Mauritius Research and Innovation Council manages Mauritius's national satellite programme. It led the development of Mauritius's first satellite. It coordinates national space and innovation projects.
specialties: Satellite programme management; research and innovation
notable_missions: MIR-SAT1 (2021, first Mauritian satellite)
notes: Mauritius has no separate space agency; this official council manages the national satellite programme. No current director verified in the research sweep.

history: Established by the National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958, signed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower on July 29, 1958; NASA opened for business on October 1, 1958, absorbing the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA). Milestones include the Mercury and Gemini programs, the Apollo Moon landings (1969-1972), Skylab, the Space Shuttle program (1981-2011), partnership in the International Space Station, and flagship science missions from Hubble to the James Webb Space Telescope; the agency's current focus is the Artemis program for a sustained return to the Moon.
key_people: Jared Isaacman, Administrator (15th; in office since December 2025)
budget_usd: US$24.4B enacted FY2026 (P.L. 119-74; NASA FY2026 spending plan shows $24,399.8M; Congress rejected the White House's $18.8B request)
specialties: human spaceflight; space science (astrophysics, planetary science, heliophysics); Earth science; aeronautics research; launch services; deep-space communications
notable_missions: Artemis program (Artemis I, 2022; Artemis II crewed lunar flyby, April 1-10, 2026); International Space Station; Mars Perseverance rover and Ingenuity helicopter; James Webb Space Telescope; Hubble Space Telescope; Europa Clipper; Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope
launch_capability: Space Launch System (SLS) for Artemis deep-space missions, plus commercial launch procurement (SpaceX Falcon 9/Heavy, ULA Vulcan, Blue Origin New Glenn)
notes: Per scope, the U.S. Space Force (a separate military service, est. 2019) is not part of NASA and is not listed as a row. Jared Isaacman was first nominated in 2025; after that nomination was withdrawn (May 2025), Sean Duffy served as acting administrator until Isaacman was confirmed and sworn in as the 15th Administrator in December 2025. The bipartisan NASA Authorization Act of 2026 authorized $24.7B for FY2026 and $25.3B for FY2027, including the first authorization of a permanent Moon base; Artemis III was redefined in 2026 as a crewed low-Earth-orbit rendezvous/docking demonstration (late 2027), with the lunar landing deferred.

founded: 2013 (1 April 2013 as the National Aerospace Development Administration; renamed September 2023)
history: Founded on 1 April 2013 as the National Aerospace Development Administration (NADA), succeeding the Korean Committee of Space Technology, and renamed the National Aerospace Technology Administration in September 2023. It runs North Korea's satellite and launch-vehicle programs, whose launch technology is dual-use and subject to UN Security Council sanctions.
key_people: Ryu Sang Hoon, Director (per encyclopedic sources; no official leadership page exists)
specialties: launch vehicles; reconnaissance and communications satellites
notable_missions: Kwangmyongsong-3 and Kwangmyongsong-4; Malligyong-1 reconnaissance satellite (2023)
launch_capability: Unha and Chollima-1 launch systems from the Sohae Satellite Launching Station
notes: No official website, public contact, published budget, or official leadership page. Launch systems are described here factually; they remain subject to UN sanctions over their dual-use nature.

agency_name: National Centre for Cartography and Remote Sensing (CNCT)
history: The National Centre for Cartography and Remote Sensing, established in 1988 under the Ministry of National Defence, is Tunisia's national institution for remote sensing and satellite programmes. It is leading Tunisia's first governmental satellite programme, reported in 2026. It develops national cartography and Earth observation capabilities.
specialties: Remote sensing; cartography; satellite programmes
notable_missions: First Tunisian governmental satellite programme (2026)
notes: Tunisia has no separate space agency; this official centre is the national space institution. No current director verified in the research sweep.

agency_name: National Commission for Aerospace Research and Development (CONIDA)
history: Founded in 1974 as Peru's national space commission under the Ministry of Defence. It develops national satellite and Earth observation capabilities. It operates the Punta Lobos ground station.
specialties: Earth observation; satellite operations
notable_missions: PeruSat-1 (2016)
notes: Current 2026 leadership not verified in official sources; the field is left blank.

history: Created on 28 May 1991 as Argentina's national space agency under the Ministry of Science. It implements the National Space Plan for satellite development and applications. It operates the Cordoba ground station and develops Earth observation satellites.

history: Formed on 1 April 2026 under the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI), subsuming the mandate and functions of the former Office for Space Technology and Industry (OSTIn). It is Singapore's first dedicated national space agency, tasked with growing the space economy, regulating space activity, and advancing national space capabilities.

specialties: space-economy development; space regulation; Earth-observation and satellite applications
notable_missions: No sovereign missions yet; heritage programs include the TeLEOS Earth-observation satellites (OSTIn era)

history: Angola's national space programme is managed by the Office for the Management of the National Space Programme (GGPEN), under the Ministry of Telecommunications, Information Technology and Media. It oversees the AngoSat communications satellite programme and national satellite capacity building.
key_people: Zolana Joao, Director General
specialties: Satellite communications; capacity building
notable_missions: AngoSat-1 (2017); AngoSat-2 (2022)
notes: Angola has no separate space agency; this is the official national space programme management office.

agency_name: National Space Research and Development Agency (NASRDA)
history: Established in 1999 to pursue the development and application of space science and technology in Nigeria. It implements the National Space Policy and Programme. It operates satellite programmes and a national network of space research centres.

agency_name: National Space System / Space Directorate, Chilean Air Force
history: Chile's national space activities are led by the Chilean Air Force, which operates the National Space System and the Space Operations Group. A National Space Centre opened in December 2025. Chile has no separate civilian space agency; the FACh Space Directorate is the official national space entity.

history: The Netherlands Space Agency was created on 3 March 2026 when the Netherlands Space Office (NSO, established 2009) was transformed into a full agency. It advises government on space policy, implements the national space agenda, and manages Dutch participation in ESA and EU space programmes. The Netherlands is a founding ESA member.

notable_missions: Dutch ESA contributions (e.g. TROPOMI instrument), national small-satellite missions, space innovation programmes
notes: Successor to the Netherlands Space Office (2009-2026). 2026 budget not published. HQ city not confirmed in located materials.

founded: 2016 (April 2016, within the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment)
history: Established in April 2016 within the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE). It regulates launch and high-altitude activities under the Outer Space and High-altitude Activities Act 2017 and develops New Zealand's commercial space sector. It is headquartered in Wellington.
key_people: Andrew Johnson, Deputy Head (identified in a March 2026 bilateral statement; the senior-most agency-specific official verified)
specialties: launch and re-entry regulation; space policy; international cooperation

history: The Norwegian Space Agency was established in 1987 as the Norwegian Space Centre when Norway joined ESA. Renamed the Norwegian Space Agency, it is a government agency under the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries. It organises Norwegian space activities, particularly with respect to ESA and the EU, and coordinates national space activities.

launch_capability: None (orbital); sounding rockets via Andoya Space
notes: 2026 budget not published by the agency. Formerly Norsk Romsenter / Norwegian Space Centre.

history: Oman adopted its National Space Policy and Executive Programme (2023-2033) in 2023. The programme is managed by the Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology (MTCIT), whose Director General of Policies and Governance heads the National Space Program. It focuses on satellite applications, the Duqm spaceport and space industry development.

notes: Oman has no separate space agency; this is the official national space programme office. No programme-specific annual budget is officially published.

specialties: Space policy; capacity building; international cooperation
notable_missions: Guaranisat-1 (2021)
notes: Phone is the agency's official switchboard number published on its public-information portal; no general email address is officially published.

It builds on university-led CubeSat programs and executes the National SPACE Development Program. It is headquartered in Quezon City.

The Office of the Director General mailbox (odg@philsa.gov.ph) is left blank as it is not clearly a general public inbox.

history: The Polish Space Agency was established on 26 September 2014 as an executive agency of the Ministry of Development and Technology. It implements Poland's Space Strategy, coordinates Polish participation in ESA and EU programmes, and supports the national space industry. Since 18 April 2026 it also acts as regulator of the space market under the Space Activities Act.

notable_missions: Polish ESA contributions, PW-Sat student satellites, EagleEye satellite (2024), national SSA centre
notes: HQ in Gdansk (ul. Trzy Lipy 3) with branches in Warsaw and Rzeszow. 2026 budget not published.

history: Portugal Space (Agencia Espacial Portuguesa) was created in 2019 as a private non-profit association with a public mission to promote and execute the Portugal Space 2030 strategy. It manages national space programmes, fosters the space ecosystem including the Azores spaceport project, and represents Portugal at ESA. Portugal has been an ESA member since 2000.

history: The Romanian Space Agency was founded in 1991 and reorganised under Government Decision 923/1995 as a public institution coordinating Romania's space activities. It designs and coordinates the National Space Programme, represents Romania in international space cooperation, and conducts research through the ROSA Research Center. Romania joined ESA in 2011.

notable_missions: Goliat nanosatellite (2012), Romanian ESA programme participation, ROSA Research Center activities

history: Russia's space agency traces to the Russian Space Agency founded by presidential decree in 1992, which became the Federal Space Agency (Roscosmos) in 2004. In 2015 it was reorganized as the State Corporation for Space Activities 'Roscosmos', consolidating the country's space industry. It operates Russia's crewed spaceflight programme, launch infrastructure and national satellite constellations.

notes: No agency-specific annual budget is officially published as a stand-alone figure; the field is left blank rather than using secondary estimates.

notable_missions: Mohammed VI-A (2017) and Mohammed VI-B (2018) Earth observation satellites

history: The Slovenian Space Office was established within the Ministry of the Economy, Tourism and Sport to coordinate national space activities and ESA engagement. Estonia became a full ESA member in 2015 and adopted a Space Act establishing licensing rules.

It develops space monitoring, remote sensing, and satellite programs, and has announced plans to send Uzbekistan's first cosmonaut to space by October 2028.

history: The Swedish National Space Agency traces its origins to 1972 and is Sweden's expert authority on civil space matters. history: The Swiss Space Office is the space division of the State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI). It implements Switzerland's space policy, manages participation in ESA - which Switzerland co-founded - and coordinates national space activities. Switzerland pursues space through international cooperation rather than a standalone agency.
